title: A Few Helpful Ideas for Resting as an Educator
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. builds on philosopher Dallas Willard's image of the body as a battery pack for the soul to argue that rest is not optional maintenance but a discipline educators must actively practice, not just experience by accident. He offers a running list of reframes rather than a single technique: resting only when fully depleted is compared to filling a gas tank only after it's empty; rest is redefined as "depressurizing" the body, mind, and will rather than sleep alone, including unstructured activities like sitting in the woods or aimlessly puttering in a garage; and rest is described as a "ceasing from striving" that can happen in ten-minute increments during a prep period or on a walk with a spouse. He includes standard sleep-hygiene basics (no screens before bed, consistent bedtime and wake time) but insists rest, paradoxically, takes intentional work to get good at, and proposes a 24-hour weekend challenge to practice ceasing from striving. The piece closes by tying rest directly back to teaching capacity: full rest is what allows a teacher to bring real intellectual, emotional, and volitional strength to the classroom.
points: Rest is reframed from "what happens when work is done" to "depressurizing the body, mind, and will" -- a broader category than sleep that includes unstructured, agenda-free activities like puttering in a garage or sitting in the woods.

Resting only after complete exhaustion is compared to filling a car's gas tank only after it runs empty -- a pattern of binge-sleeping and getting sick that Stuart identifies from his own past habits and explicitly rejects.

"Ceasing from striving" is offered as the operative definition of rest, achievable in short doses (a ten-minute walk during a prep period, a short walk with a spouse) rather than requiring long blocks of free time.

A 24-hour weekend challenge -- picking any 24-hour window to consciously cease from striving -- is proposed as the fastest practical way to build the skill of resting well, since Stuart argues rest, paradoxically, requires intentional practice to get good at.
quotes: Notice that your soul isn't a wispy little ghost inside you that floats up to heaven when you die, like it's portrayed in the movies. It's actually your whole person.

Resting only when you're completely exhausted is like filling your car's gas tank only after it's empty. I used to deprive myself of sleep — staying up too late for extra work time or extra free time — for days on end, and then once my body had had it I'd binge on sleep over a weekend or I'd get a cold.
Think of rest as depressurizing the body, mind, and will. In other words, it's not just sleep. It's sitting in the woods or a park for twenty minutes after a hard day of teaching.
Another way to think of rest: a ceasing from striving. Sleep is a great example of this ceasing as even our consciousness stops striving and whole parts of our body shut down.
Resting well takes work. Like lots of life's truths, it's paradoxical. But like all human pursuits, intentional practice is required for getting good at resting.
One of the quickest ways to get better at rest is to challenge yourself to 24 hours straight of it each weekend.
And finally: getting great at rest means we can get awesome at education. Remember the thing I started with, about how the body is a battery pack for the soul?
